# The review's three high findings, closed, and four things nobody had named

RED is record 23 and GREEN is record 24, `pnpm --filter @seen/core test` both times, 11 failed and 46
passed then 57 passed. The RED reproduced the reviewer's own executions as tests rather than trusting its
description. In the runner's words: "a signed-in user of the tenant deleted the tenant row, and the
cascade took the trade record with it: of the 2 audit events and 1 order the tenant had, 0 audit events
and 0 orders are left"; "the tenant wrote its own settlement line and its own credited claim, which is a
billable event created by a person rather than ingested"; "the tenant zeroed and voided its own invoice";
"the tenant deleted its own signed statement"; "58 table and role pairs hold privileges the trade record
does not intend"; and, for the two assertion holes, "A second permissive policy on public.evidence reading
'using (true)' exposes every tenant's evidence, and the tenancy assertion reported nothing at all".

**The decision this rests on, taken by the orchestrating session and recorded before the work:** `anon`
and `authenticated` get select only on every trade-record table, and every write goes through the API with
the service role, because the architecture has server components reading Postgres through RLS and nothing
in the product writes from the client. Tenant deletion, and therefore erasure on request, becomes a
service-role action, which SEEN-083 owns. `anon` loses select too, as defence in depth: it carries no
tenant claim so RLS already yields nothing, and a table that later loses its policy should not also be
readable by the unauthenticated.

The measured result after `pnpm db:reset`, from `relacl` rather than from intent: `anon` holds nothing at
all on all 29 tables, with no ACL entry; `authenticated` holds select on 29 and nothing else;
`service_role` holds select and insert on 29, and update, delete and truncate on 28, not `audit_events`.
Probed as the service role in a rolled-back transaction: insert a tenant, insert an audit event, insert and
update a connection, delete the tenant, all accepted, so the revoke is not over-broad and the erasure
cascade is still reachable by the server. The revoke had to be per-table over `pg_class` rather than a
blanket statement, because the grants were not the only source: Supabase's default ACL for schema public
had granted the same four privileges at table-creation time. The migration ends with a self-check that
raises if a client-bound role still holds anything unintended, and not with a blanket grant, which is the
trap recorded at record 16.

F1 is closed inside the ticket's own files, on one verified fact: CI's monorepo job starts Supabase before
`pnpm turbo run test`, so making the package's `test` script the whole suite puts the tenancy guard in CI
with no change to `turbo.json` or the workflow. `test:unit` keeps the database-free path.

F5, F6 and F8 are closed together: the tenancy assertion now reads the whole permissive policy set per
table and both `qual` and `with_check`, the privilege assertion covers all 29 tables and all three roles
from `aclexplode`, and every catalogue assertion of that shape is guarded against passing on an empty
schema. Three probe tests inject the exact failures, an empty schema, a `using (true)` policy and a
`with check (true)` policy, and require the suite to notice.

**Four things neither the reviewer nor the orchestrator named.**

1. **The coverage command this project has been using measures nothing.** `pnpm --filter @seen/core test
   -- --coverage.enabled --coverage.reporter=json-summary` exits 0, but pnpm forwards the literal `--`, so
   vitest parks the flags after it and never enables coverage: `packages/core/coverage/coverage-summary.json`
   was still the 23 September file after the run. `pnpm exec vitest run --coverage.enabled ...` writes a
   fresh summary. This predates the change, the old `test` script had the same problem, and the
   consequence is that the harness's coverage phase has been reading a stale file rather than failing. It
   needs a harness ticket: `harness/` is not in this ticket's files.
2. **`harness guard` cannot see this ticket's slice plan.** On this branch `guard supabase/migrations/...`
   answers `allowed: true` with rule `no-slice-plan` and the reason "No accepted slice plan yet for
   SEEN-008", while `status --brief` says three of three slices are done. So the guard has been allowing
   every path on this ticket for a reason unrelated to the plan, which is the opposite failure from the
   exact-match refusal recorded at records 10, 13 and 16 on the other branch. Both belong in the same
   harness ticket.
3. **Default privileges stay wide for tables that do not exist yet.** `pg_default_acl` still grants the
   four write privileges to `anon` and `authenticated` on new tables in schema public, for both `postgres`
   and `supabase_admin`, so SEEN-014's next table will be born writable by the role a browser is bound to.
   The new privilege assertion fails loudly when that happens, which is detection and not prevention.
   Narrowing it with `alter default privileges` was deliberately not done: it was not in the decision
   recorded above and it changes every future migration.
4. The migration's first self-check draft failed the reset because the table owner legitimately holds
   update, delete and truncate on `audit_events`: it is the trigger and not the privilege that refuses
   those to the owner. The check is scoped to the three Data API roles and the comment says why.
